title: Electrolit for Hangover: Does It Work and How to Drink It
excerpt: Does Electrolit help a hangover? What's in it, what it can and can't fix, how much to drink, when to drink it, and how it compares with Pedialyte and Gatorade.
metaDescription: Does Electrolit help a hangover? What it can and can't fix, how much to drink, best timing, and how it compares with Pedialyte and Gatorade.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Electrolit is a good drink to have on hand the morning after, but it is not a hangover cure. It's an oral rehydration drink, the same basic kind of product as Pedialyte, so it replaces the water and salt you lose from drinking, vomiting, or diarrhea more efficiently than plain water does. That helps with thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness, and some of the "drained" feeling. It does nothing for the other big drivers of a hangover: poor sleep, inflammation, an irritated stomach, and the by-products your body makes as it breaks down alcohol. Drink one bottle slowly, eat something, and give it a few hours. If you only had a couple of drinks and feel fine, water and breakfast will usually do the same job for less money.

**The quick rules:**

- **Best use:** the morning after a heavy night, especially if you were sick, have diarrhea, or feel dizzy when you stand up.
- **How much:** one bottle (about 21 fl oz / 625 mL), sipped over an hour or two, is plenty for most healthy adults. Follow it with water.
- **Before bed:** a few glasses of water plus some of an Electrolit can help, but there is no good evidence that drinking it before bed prevents a hangover.
- **Which flavor:** the one you'll actually finish. The formula is similar across flavors, so check the label if you're watching sugar.
- **Skip it or ask a doctor first if** you have kidney disease, heart failure, or have been told to limit salt, fluids, or potassium.

> **When to see a doctor instead of reaching for a bottle.** Electrolit is for mild dehydration. **Get medical care if** you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, you haven't urinated in 8 hours or more, you feel faint or dizzy when you stand, you're confused, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, or you have severe belly pain. **Call 911 right away** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken up, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no drink fixes that. If you drink heavily most days and get shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or start seeing or hearing things that aren't there within a day or two of stopping, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Tell a doctor or go to urgent care rather than trying to treat it at home.

## What Electrolit Actually Is

Electrolit is a ready-to-drink **oral rehydration solution**, which doctors shorten to ORS. It's made by a Mexican pharmaceutical company and has been sold in Mexico for years as a *suero oral* (people usually just say *suero*). In the last several years it has spread across US grocery stores, gas stations, and big-box stores, usually in a tall plastic bottle of about 21 fluid ounces (625 mL) and a long list of flavors.

An ORS is a drink built around a specific balance of salt and sugar. The idea goes back to research in the 1960s and 70s showing that the small intestine absorbs sodium and glucose together, and pulls water in with them. When the ratio is right, the gut can absorb fluid even when someone is losing a lot of it, which is why ORS became the standard treatment for dehydration from cholera and other diarrheal illness. The World Health Organization and UNICEF publish a reference formula that's still used worldwide.

Retail drinks like Electrolit and Pedialyte follow the same principle with a gentler recipe meant for mild dehydration. That's the key difference from a sports drink. Gatorade and similar drinks are built mainly to fuel exercise, so they carry more sugar and less sodium. An ORS carries more sodium and less sugar, which is the better mix for getting fluid back into your body.

### What's in a bottle

Electrolit's label lists water, glucose (dextrose), and a set of mineral salts that supply **sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, and magnesium**, along with flavorings and, in most versions, colorings and a sweetener. The exact amounts vary by flavor, by the country the bottle was made for, and by version, since the formula has been adjusted over time. The honest advice is to **read the Nutrition Facts panel on the bottle you're holding** instead of trusting a number from any website, including this one.

In general terms:

- **Sodium** is in the oral rehydration range, well above a typical sports drink. This is the electrolyte that matters most for holding on to water.
- **Potassium** is included, which is useful if you've been vomiting or have diarrhea, since both drain it.
- **Sugar** is moderate. It's there to help absorption, not just for taste, and it's much less than a soda or a full-sugar sports drink.
- **Calcium and magnesium** are present in small amounts. They're a nice extra, but a single bottle is not a meaningful magnesium supplement.

## Does Electrolit Help a Hangover?

It helps with **part** of a hangover. To see which part, it helps to know what a hangover actually is.

### The part Electrolit can help with: fluid and salt loss

Alcohol makes you urinate more than you drink. It does this by suppressing **vasopressin**, a hormone (also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of that signal, more water passes straight through. Add a night of sweating in a hot bar, not drinking much water, and maybe vomiting, and you can wake up genuinely low on fluid and salt.

That shows up as:

- Thirst and a dry, sticky mouth
- Lightheadedness, especially when you stand up quickly
- Dark yellow urine, or not much of it
- A dull headache that can be partly from low fluid
- Feeling weak and flat

An ORS like Electrolit replaces water and sodium faster than plain water, because the sodium and glucose pull water across the gut wall. If you were sick during the night or have diarrhea the next day, that difference matters more, since you're also losing potassium and other salts.

### The part it can't touch

Here's what the marketing tends to leave out. Researchers who study hangovers have found that how dehydrated someone is, and their blood electrolyte levels, don't line up closely with how bad they feel. In other words, dehydration is a real piece of a hangover, but usually not the biggest piece. The rest comes from:

- **Acetaldehyde**, the toxic chemical your liver makes when it first breaks down alcohol
- **Inflammation**, a body-wide immune response that alcohol triggers
- **Poor-quality sleep**, because alcohol disrupts the deeper and dreaming stages of sleep later in the night
- **Stomach irritation**, which drives nausea and loss of appetite
- **Low blood sugar** in some people, especially after drinking without eating
- **Congeners**, the extra compounds in darker drinks like red wine, whiskey, and brandy

No electrolyte drink fixes those. So the fair way to put it is this: there is no good evidence that Electrolit, or any electrolyte drink, cures or prevents a hangover. It's a sensible way to fix the dehydration part, and that part can make a real difference to how you feel. Our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) covers the science of what drinking does to your fluid and salt balance in more detail.

## How to Drink Electrolit When You're Hungover

How you drink it matters almost as much as what's in it, especially if your stomach is unsettled.

1. **Start with small sips.** If you feel queasy, take a few sips every few minutes rather than a long pull. A full stomach of cold liquid is an easy way to bring it all back up.
2. **Drink it cold.** Most people find it tastes better chilled, and cold drinks tend to be easier to tolerate when you're nauseated.
3. **Spread one bottle over an hour or two.** Your gut can only absorb so much at once. Slow and steady works better than fast.
4. **Follow with water.** Once the bottle is done, switch to plain water for the rest of the day. You don't need a second bottle unless you're still losing fluid.
5. **Eat when you can.** Toast, crackers, rice, bananas, eggs, or a brothy soup give you carbohydrate, protein, and more salt. In Mexico, a bottle of *suero* often goes alongside menudo, chilaquiles, or a hot caldo. Our guide to [traditional Mexican hangover remedies](/never-hungover/traditional-mexican-hangover-remedies-vs-modern-supplements) looks at what those classic fixes do and don't do.
6. **Rest.** Sleep you lost to alcohol is one of the biggest reasons you feel bad. Electrolit won't replace a nap.

### If you're vomiting

If you can't keep anything down, wait 15 to 30 minutes after the last time you were sick, then start again with a teaspoon or a small sip every few minutes. If that stays down for half an hour, slowly increase. Some people find frozen ORS easier than drinking it, so pouring Electrolit into an ice cube tray or popsicle mold the night before isn't a bad idea. If you still can't keep fluids down after several hours, that's a reason to get medical care, not to keep trying harder. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more on settling your stomach.

## Electrolit Before Bed or Before Drinking?

People often ask whether it's better to drink Electrolit before bed, before going out, or the next morning. Here's a practical view.

**Before going out:** there's no good evidence that "pre-loading" electrolytes stops a hangover. What does help is eating a proper meal, which slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream. If you want to start the night well hydrated, a glass or two of water does most of the work.

**During the night:** alternating each alcoholic drink with a glass of water is one of the simplest habits that helps. It slows your drinking and limits fluid loss. You don't need an electrolyte drink for this, though some people keep one handy at a long event in the heat.

**Before bed:** a reasonable move if you feel very thirsty or you've been sick. Drinking half a bottle with some water before sleep can ease the dry-mouth, pounding-thirst feeling in the morning. Just don't expect it to block the other hangover symptoms. Drinking a large amount of anything right before bed also means more trips to the bathroom, which cuts into sleep you badly need.

**The next morning:** this is when Electrolit tends to be most useful, because you can tell how much you actually need. If you wake up dry, dizzy, or after a rough night of vomiting, that's the moment to reach for it.

For a fuller breakdown of timing, see our guide on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking).

## Electrolit Pros and Cons for Hangovers

Here's an honest look at where it shines and where it falls short.

**What's good about it:**

- **It's a real oral rehydration drink.** The sodium and sugar balance is designed for rehydration, not for fueling exercise.
- **Many people find it easier to drink than Pedialyte.** This is its biggest advantage. A drink you'll actually finish beats a slightly better one that makes you gag.
- **The bottle is large.** About 21 fl oz is a sensible single serving for an adult the morning after.
- **Lots of flavors.** If one tastes off when you're queasy, another might not.
- **Easy to find.** Gas stations and convenience stores often carry it, which matters at 9 a.m. when you don't want to go far.
- **Ready to drink.** No mixing, no measuring.

**What's less good:**

- **It's not cheap per serving.** A single bottle usually costs more than a serving of electrolyte powder, and much more than water and a salty snack.
- **It still has sugar.** Not a lot compared with soda, but worth counting if you have diabetes or are watching calories.
- **Colorings and sweeteners.** Some people prefer to avoid them. Check the ingredient list on your flavor.
- **Lots of plastic.** One-use bottles add up if you drink it often.
- **Limited track record in young children compared with Pedialyte.** For a sick child, ask your pediatrician which product to use.
- **It only treats one part of a hangover.** It won't help much if your main problems are poor sleep, a headache from other causes, or general misery.

## Electrolit vs Other Hangover Drinks

You'll find several options on the same shelf. Here's how Electrolit compares for a hangover in plain terms.

| Drink | What it is | How it compares for a hangover |
|---|---|---|
| **Electrolit** | Oral rehydration solution | Good rehydration, easy taste for many people, bigger bottle |
| **Pedialyte** | Oral rehydration solution | Very similar job; longer medical track record, more formats; some adults dislike the taste |
| **Gatorade (regular)** | Sports drink | More sugar, less sodium; fine for mild thirst, weaker choice if you're vomiting or have diarrhea |
| **Liquid I.V. and similar powders** | Drink mix with electrolytes and sugar | Cheaper per serving, portable; you mix it yourself; formulas vary |
| **Coconut water** | Natural juice | High in potassium but fairly low in sodium; pleasant, but not a full ORS |
| **Plain water** | Water | Free and often enough after a few drinks; slower if you've lost a lot of fluid and salt |

A few notes on the closest comparisons:

- **Electrolit vs Pedialyte.** They do about the same job. Choose on taste, price, and format. For babies or young children who are sick, Pedialyte has the longer pediatric track record. We cover this in depth in [Electrolit vs Pedialyte](/never-hungover/electrolit-vs-pedialyte).
- **Electrolit vs Gatorade.** Gatorade is fine if you're just thirsty, but its higher sugar and lower sodium make it a weaker rehydration drink, especially with diarrhea. See our guide to [Gatorade for a hangover](/never-hungover/gatorade-for-hangover).
- **Electrolit vs Liquid I.V.** Both can work. Powders are cheaper and travel well, but you're relying on mixing them with the right amount of water. Our [Liquid I.V. for hangover](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover) guide covers the trade-offs.
- **Electrolit vs coconut water.** Coconut water tastes good and has plenty of potassium, but usually much less sodium than an ORS. Read more in our [coconut water for hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) guide.

For a side-by-side of all the major brands, see our [electrolyte drinks for hangovers comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared).

## Can You Make Your Own Instead?

Yes. A homemade oral rehydration drink costs pennies and works on the same principle. The classic home recipe uses clean water, a small amount of salt, and some sugar, mixed in careful proportions. Getting the ratio right matters, because too much salt or too much sugar can make things worse, especially for children or anyone with diarrhea. Our [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) guide gives tested recipes and explains the measurements.

For a typical hangover in a healthy adult, the gap between a homemade drink and a bottle of Electrolit is small. The bottle wins on convenience and taste. The homemade version wins on price.

## Which Electrolit Flavor or Version Is Best for a Hangover?

There's no hangover-specific flavor. The formula is broadly similar across the regular line, so the best flavor is simply the one you like enough to finish when you feel rough. A few practical tips:

- **Milder flavors can be easier when you're nauseated.** Some people find strong, very sweet, or very sour flavors harder to keep down.
- **Lower-sugar versions exist in some markets.** These still give you water and salt, which helps. Without as much glucose, they're a bit less efficient at pulling water in, but for a mild hangover the difference is minor.
- **Check the label for caffeine-free.** Regular Electrolit doesn't contain caffeine, but if you're comparing it with other "hydration" or "energy" drinks, make sure you know what you're getting. Caffeine on top of a hangover can worsen jitters and an upset stomach for some people.
- **Keep one in the fridge.** If you know you have a big night coming, chilling a bottle ahead of time means it's ready when you need it.

## How Much Electrolit Is Too Much?

For most healthy adults, one bottle the morning after, followed by water, is plenty. Drinking several bottles a day when you don't need them just adds extra salt and sugar.

There are a few groups who should be more careful or ask a doctor before using any electrolyte drink regularly:

- People with **kidney disease**, since the kidneys manage sodium and potassium
- People with **heart failure** or **high blood pressure** who have been told to limit salt or fluids
- People taking medicines that raise potassium, such as some blood pressure medicines (ACE inhibitors and ARBs) or potassium-sparing diuretics
- People with **diabetes**, who should count the sugar and talk to their care team about which rehydration drink to use when they're sick
- **Pregnant** people who are vomiting a lot, who should talk to their doctor or midwife

It's also possible, though uncommon, to drink too much fluid overall. Forcing down huge amounts of any liquid in a short time can lower the sodium in your blood. Drink to thirst and spread your fluids out rather than trying to "flush" a hangover with gallons.

## When a Hangover Is More Than Dehydration

Most hangovers ease within a day. A few situations are worth taking more seriously.

- **Symptoms that last more than a day**, or that get worse instead of better, are worth mentioning to a doctor.
- **Severe belly pain**, especially in the upper middle of your belly spreading to your back, can be a sign of pancreatitis, which heavy drinking can trigger. Get checked.
- **Vomiting blood**, or what looks like coffee grounds, needs urgent care.
- **Confusion, a very slow or irregular heartbeat, or fainting** need medical attention.
- **Shaking, sweating, anxiety, and a racing heart a day or so after stopping** in someone who drinks heavily most days can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover. Withdrawal can become dangerous, so see a doctor rather than trying to rehydrate your way through it.

If you notice you're reaching for an Electrolit most weekends, it's also worth looking at the drinking itself. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence: eating first, pacing, alternating with water, picking lighter drinks, and protecting your sleep. Our guide to [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers the rest of the rehydration toolkit.

## Where DHM Fits In

Electrolit deals with the water and salt side of a hangover. It does nothing about alcohol metabolism, which is where some people look at supplements. The most talked-about one is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*).

Here's an honest summary of where DHM stands:

- Most of the research comes from **animal and lab studies**, which suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and its by-products, and may support the liver.
- There's a small amount of **human data**, including a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease that found improvements in some liver markers. That study wasn't about hangovers.
- There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people, and it does not make heavy drinking safe.

Some people combine the two approaches: a DHM supplement with their drinks and an oral rehydration drink like Electrolit the next morning. If you want to try DHM, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) and [dosage calculator](/dhm-dosage-calculator) cover how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicine, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Electrolit is a ready-to-drink oral rehydration solution, the same basic type of drink as Pedialyte.
- It helps with the **dehydration part** of a hangover: thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness, and fluid lost from vomiting or diarrhea.
- There is no good evidence that it cures or prevents a hangover, because most hangover symptoms come from other causes like poor sleep, inflammation, and acetaldehyde.
- Sip one cold bottle slowly over an hour or two, then switch to water and eat something.
- Pick the flavor you'll finish. Check the label if you're watching sugar.
- Ask a doctor first if you have kidney or heart problems or take medicines that raise potassium.
- If you can't keep fluids down, have severe pain, are confused, or someone can't be woken, get medical help instead.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Electrolit good for a hangover?**

It's a good choice for the dehydration side of a hangover. Electrolit is an oral rehydration drink, so it replaces water and salt more efficiently than plain water, which helps with thirst, dry mouth, and lightheadedness. It won't fix the headache, nausea, or fatigue that come from poor sleep, inflammation, and alcohol by-products, and there is no good evidence that it cures or prevents a hangover.

**Should I drink Electrolit before bed or the next morning?**

The next morning is usually the most useful time, because you can tell how much you need. Drinking some before bed with a glass of water is fine if you're very thirsty or were sick, but there is no good evidence it prevents a hangover, and drinking a lot right before sleep means more trips to the bathroom.

**How much Electrolit should I drink for a hangover?**

For most healthy adults, one bottle (about 21 fl oz) sipped slowly over an hour or two is enough, followed by plain water for the rest of the day. More isn't better. If you have kidney disease, heart failure, or have been told to limit salt, fluids, or potassium, ask a doctor before using electrolyte drinks.

**Is Electrolit better than Pedialyte for a hangover?**

They do about the same job. Both are oral rehydration solutions with similar amounts of sodium and moderate sugar. Many people find Electrolit easier to drink and like the bigger bottle, while Pedialyte has a longer track record, especially for children, and comes in more formats like powders and freezer pops. Pick the one you'll actually finish.

**Is Electrolit better than Gatorade for a hangover?**

Usually, yes, if you're genuinely dehydrated. Gatorade is a sports drink with more sugar and less sodium, while Electrolit is designed for rehydration. If you were vomiting or have diarrhea, an oral rehydration drink like Electrolit is the better choice. If you're just a bit thirsty, either one, or water, will do.

**Does Electrolit have caffeine?**

Regular Electrolit does not contain caffeine. It's made of water, glucose, and mineral salts that supply sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, and magnesium, plus flavorings. Check the label on any specific product, since formulas can vary by flavor and country.

**Can Electrolit help if I've been throwing up after drinking?**

Yes, this is one of the situations where it's most useful, because vomiting drains both water and salts. Wait 15 to 30 minutes after the last time you were sick, then take small sips every few minutes and slowly increase. If you can't keep any fluids down for several hours, are vomiting blood, or feel confused or faint, get medical care.

**Is it safe to drink Electrolit every day?**

For most healthy people, an occasional bottle is fine, but daily use when you're not losing fluid just adds extra salt and sugar you don't need. People with kidney disease, heart failure, high blood pressure on a salt limit, diabetes, or who take medicines that raise potassium should ask a doctor before drinking electrolyte drinks regularly.
